Learning Objectives
Describe the role of systemic therapy in the management of soft-tissue sarcoma.
Identify common soft-tissue sarcomas managed via chemotherapy.
Understand the manner in which chemotherapy is used to manage soft-tissue sarcoma.
Review the role of systemic therapy as part of a comprehensive treatment plan for soft-tissue
sarcoma.
Differentiate systemic treatment with curative intent from systemic treatment with palliative
intent.

Soft-tissue sarcomas (STS) represent a rare, heterogeneous group of malignancies derived
from connective tissue (mesoderm), with more than 100 distinct subtypes.1
Tumors of the same histologic phenotype (ie, subtypes of rhabdomyosarcoma) may have
different underlying genetic abnormalities that can alter management and prognosis. In
addition, some tumors are dedifferentiated to the point that their family cannot be
determined, and they are classified as undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma. This
heterogeneity and rarity make finding effective systemic treatment options a challenge.2
The management, survival, and treatment options for STS have progressed slowly since the
1980s, especially compared with the remarkable advancements made in other common
malignancies, such as breast and lung cancer; however, new and exciting trials include
investigation of targeted therapeutic agents.3,4
Most STSs are managed via radiation therapy (preoperatively or postoperatively) and surgery,
with a few exceptions.5
Systemic therapy for STS generally is considered in the following scenarios:
Large high-grade tumors; however, this is controversial.6,7
STS with particular sensitivity to systemic therapy (ie, synovial sarcoma)
STS with targetable genetic mutations
Unresectable or marginally resectable tumors
Metastatic disease8
Epidemiology
Sarcomas are rare, representing fewer than 1% of all malignancies.
The standard of care for the management of STS is treatment in a tertiary referral center. A
multidisciplinary approach is required to optimize patient outcomes.9

Epidemiology
According to the National Institutes of Health Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End
Results database, approximately 13,100 new cases of STS will be diagnosed in the United
States in 2020, with approximately 5,300 deaths. The 5-year overall survival is

Systemic Therapy
Chemotherapy
Targeted therapy
Development

Systemic Therapy
Cytotoxic chemotherapy indiscriminately halts cell division (mitosis) and induces cell
death by promoting apoptosis. Because cancer is uncontrolled cell growth,
chemotherapy is used to kill the rapidly dividing tumor cells. In general, tumors with fast
growth rates are more sensitive to chemotherapy; however, many of the adverse effects
result from collateral damage to the rapidly dividing cells in the body, such as those in
bone marrow, the gastrointestinal lining, and hair follicles, leading to myelosuppression,
gastrointestinal upset, and hair loss, respectively.
The mechanisms of action of chemotherapy agents vary; however, all cytotoxic agents
disrupt the cell cycle and thereby interrupt cell division (Figure 1).

The first successful targeted therapy for sarcoma occurred nearly 20 years ago in a
woman with a metastatic gastrointestinal stromal tumor. Treatment via chemotherapy
had failed, and the patient was treated with the use of imatinib, a tyrosine kinase
inhibitor, which resulted in a considerable reduction in the size of her tumors.11
A tremendous surge in the development of targeted therapies for sarcoma has occurred
in the past 5 to 10 years12,13 (Figure 2).

Cytotoxic Chemotherapy
Chemotherapy has a limited role in the management of surgically resectable STS,9,14 with a
few notable exceptions.
Adverse effects

Cytotoxic Chemotherapy
Chemotherapy treatment usually depends on an anthracycline (doxorubicin)-based
regimen.15 The addition of ifosfamide has shown to be beneficial in multiple randomized
controlled trials.16

Adverse effects may be severe and remain a major concern for patients.17 They include
short-term reactions, such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, mucositis, constipation, hair
loss, and immunosuppression. Nausea and vomiting are two of the most noteworthy
and feared aspects of chemotherapy.18
Long-term sequelae also may result in peripheral neuropathy, cognitive impairment, and
decline in fertility. Almost 50% of patients will experience a serious adverse reaction.19
Targeted Therapy
Targeted agents have shown effectiveness in many sarcoma subtypes; however, currently,
they are not first-line therapy for localized resectable disease.20
Combined therapy

Targeted Therapy
Targeted agents may prove useful in tumors that are classically resistant to
chemotherapy, such as alveolar soft part sarcoma, epithelioid sarcoma, and clear cell
sarcoma.20,21 (Table 1; Resource 1)
Currently, several clinical trials are evaluating the effectiveness of multiagent therapy
(chemotherapy and targeted agents).7,12

Management Goals: Curative Intent Versus Palliation
Curative intent
Palliative intent (prolonging life)

Management Goals: Curative Intent Versus Palliation
The goal in patients with isolated and localized sarcoma is treatment with curative intent.
Chemotherapy can play two primary roles in this regard. First, systemic treatment may
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:46 AM
AAOS | Systemic Management of Soft-Tissue Sarcoma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004042
8/15

shrink the tumor, making it easier to resect and thereby improve surgical margins.
Second, it may be used to manage micro-metastases that may be clinically undetectable
on presentation. The role of adjuvant chemotherapy in patients with resectable STS is
marginal in terms of local recurrence, development of metastasis, and overall survival;16
however, recent data suggest that adding chemotherapy to manage high-grade
sarcomas slightly improves distant control.22 This small benefit must be weighed against
systemic toxicity.
In some instances, excision of distant metastasis (metastasectomy) is indicated if
complete resection is possible. For example, in the lungs, this would involve a wedge
resection or, in more advanced disease, a pneumonectomy. Resection of metastatic
disease is the single most important factor that determines overall survival.23
If sarcoma is metastatic on presentation or a patient secondarily develops distant
metastases and a cure is not possible, then systemic therapy is used with palliative
intent to prolong life in the setting of a terminal illness. Metastatic sarcoma is associated
with a poor prognosis, with overall survival of approximately 12 to 15 months.24
Recent data suggest that multiagent therapy may be beneficial with regard to survival
compared with monotherapy.7 Some patients may forgo chemotherapy or other
systemic treatments to focus on quality, rather than quantity, of life because of the
adverse effects of various treatment options.
Chemosensitive Soft-Tissue Sarcomas
Currently, the role of systemic treatment in STS is limited primarily to metastatic disease, with
a few notable exceptions.
These subtypes of sarcoma are particularly sensitive to chemotherapy, and management may
involve a combination of systemic therapy, radiation therapy, and surgery.
The treatment plan for each patient is unique and determined by a multidisciplinary team of
experts. Protocols may vary, depending on patient and tumor characteristics and institutional
expertise.
Synovial sarcoma


Chemosensitive Soft-Tissue Sarcomas
Synovial sarcoma is somewhat of a misnomer because it usually does not arise from or
involve synovium. Rather, it histologic appearance resembles that of synovium. Its
pathognomonic translocation t(X;18) results in the fusion product SYT-SSX1, SYT-SSX2, or
SYT-SSX4. Standard management generally includes radiation therapy and surgery and
may include chemotherapy25 (Figure 3).
Figure 3 T2-weighted axial MRIs with contrast of the femur of a patient with synovial
sarcoma obtained at the time of diagnosis (A) and after neoadjuvant chemoradiation
therapy (B). A remarkable decrease in the size of the tumor is observed; however, the
femoral neurovascular bundle remained encased and was resected with the specimen
during surgical management. (Courtesy of Frank E. Chiarappa, MD, San Diego, CA.)

Rhabdomyosarcoma accounts for approximately 40% of childhood STS. It has a unique
staging system compared with other STS. Location, type (alveolar versus embryonal), and
specific translocations (ie, PAX3-FOXO1 versus PAX7-FOXO1) are associated with
prognostic implications.26 The sarcoma typically is managed via a combination of
chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and surgery.
Ewing sarcoma typically occurs in the pelvis or long bones of young patients but also
may present in an extra-skeletal location. The Ewing family of tumors are particularly
chemosensitive, and treatment protocols generally include chemotherapy with surgery
and/or radiation therapy.
Chemotherapy may play a role in the management of certain subtypes of liposarcoma,
especially if it may facilitate less morbid surgical management or if adequate margins
cannot be achieved. Myxoid liposarcoma has a predilection to metastasize to the viscera
and neuroaxis; therefore, staging may include imaging these areas.
Alveolar soft part sarcoma is a highly vascular tumor that does not respond well to
chemotherapy or radiation therapy. Because of its angiogenic component, recent trials
have shown encouraging outcomes with the use of vascular endothelial growth factor
inhibitors.27
Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans is a cutaneous sarcoma that rarely metastasizes
(5%). Imatinib is indicated if a tumor is not surgically resectable or if shrinking the tumor
(occasionally by 20%-30%) to allow surgical resection.28,29
Effectiveness of Systemic Therapy

Effectiveness of Systemic Therapy
The effectiveness of systemic therapy can be evaluated via clinical, radiographic, and/or
histologic assessment. Tumors that are large or causing mass effect may cause pain,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:46 AM
AAOS | Systemic Management of Soft-Tissue Sarcoma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004042
11/15

swelling, or neuropathy. In general, symptom improvement is associated with a
favorable response (ie, tumor shrinkage).
Advanced imaging studies can be obtained objectively evaluate the response of the
tumor. Accurate measurements can be determined via MRI or CT, and certain
characteristics, such as decreased edema and cystic changes, may represent a good
response. Metabolic activity of tumors may be evaluated via positron emission
tomography, with a decrease in the maximum standardized uptake value correlating
with treatment response.
If a tumor is resected after systemic treatment, the pathologist reports the percentage of
necrosis (out of 100). A favorable response to management is more than 90% necrosis,
meaning less than 10% viable tumor is present in the resected specimen, which refers to
the effectiveness of the neoadjuvant treatment. Tumor necrosis of less than 90% is
associated with increased local recurrence and decreased overall survival in patients
with STS.30
